payload.body_text:
An agent can follow its instructions perfectly and still become dangerous overnight.

Doctrine has a half-life: the period in which the organization’s diagnosis, tradeoffs, and rules remain valid. When that map goes stale, an agent does not become less confident. It keeps acting coherently from premises the organization no longer holds.

Imagine a pricing agent authorized to issue quotes under a growth strategy. The strategy changes. Its permission does not. Now it is making valid decisions for a company that no longer exists.

Permissioning cannot be a one-time capability approval. It must include recurring review of the doctrine authorizing that capability—and a named owner accountable when doctrine ages but the agent keeps acting.

Autonomous permissions should inherit the doctrine’s expiration date. If the map expires, the authority expires with it.

novel_idea.topic_thesis: Autonomous permissions should expire with the doctrine’s half-life, because an agent still acting after its governing map goes stale becomes a confident source of incoherence.
novel_idea.angle: Shift permissioning from a one-time capability approval to recurring review of whether the doctrine authorizing that capability is still current.
novel_idea.hook: The dangerous agent isn’t the one that fails its launch review. It’s the one that passed—and kept acting after the strategy changed.
novel_idea.argument_summary: An agent can remain technically capable, compliant, and internally consistent even after the doctrine governing it has stopped matching reality. Because doctrine has a half-life, initial alignment cannot justify permanent authority. Once the map expires, faithful execution becomes coherent wrongness: obsolete premises are converted into customer messages, code, spending, or commitments at machine speed. Permissions therefore need stop conditions and recurring revalidation tied to doctrine version, freshness, and ownership—especially where actions touch customers, money, compliance, production systems, or irreversible promises.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest prior post establishes a Context Checksum as an entry gate before permissions increase. This argument addresses a different failure mechanism and operator decision: authority that was correctly granted can become dangerous later because doctrine expires while permissions persist. The substantive delta is from one-time alignment testing to time-bounded, doctrine-dependent authority with mandatory revalidation.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The Coherence Ceiling defines doctrine half-life as the period before doctrine becomes stale through drift or world change. Auteurs, Agents, Actors states that agents require current doctrine, permissions, evaluations, stop conditions, escalation triggers, and feedback paths, and warns that stale doctrine can produce coherent wrongness. Appendix B requires doctrine versioning, permission levels, deletion of stale workflows, and doctrine updates when reality falsifies the map. The Ashby discussion adds that a stale model can turn the regulator itself into a disturbance generator.
